title: After a hailstorm: what to check before you call your insurer
excerpt: Hail damage is easy to miss from the ground. Here's what to look for, what to photograph, and why the date matters.
content:
Most hail damage can't be seen from the street. A roof can look fine and still have bruised shingles that start leaking a year later, after your claim window has closed. Here's what to do in the first few days.

1. Note the date and the size

Write down the date and roughly how big the hail was: pea, quarter or golf ball. Your insurer will ask, and it's the first thing an adjuster checks against the weather records.

2. Look at the soft things first

Walk round the house and look at gutters, downspouts, window screens, the air conditioner fins and the car. Dents there are the easiest proof that hail big enough to hurt shingles came down at your address.

3. Photograph from the ground

Take photos of anything dented and any shingle pieces or granules in the gutters or at the bottom of downspouts. Please don't climb up yourself: wet shingles and a ladder are how most storm injuries happen.

4. Get a free inspection before you file

We'll come out, go up, mark every hit and send you a photo report the same day. If there's no real damage we'll tell you, so you don't file a claim you don't need. If there is, the report is what your insurer wants to see.

title: Five signs your roof needs replacing, not repairing
excerpt: Curling shingles, bald patches and a sagging ridge. How to tell when patching stops making sense.
content:
A good repair can add years to a roof. But some roofs are past it, and patching them just means paying twice. These are the signs we look for.

Shingles curling or cupping

Edges turning up or the middle sinking in means the shingles have dried out. They'll crack in the next freeze and blow off in the next storm.

Bald patches and granules in the gutters

The gritty granules protect shingles from the sun. Once they wash off, the shingle underneath wears out fast.

A roof over 20 years old

Most asphalt roofs here last 18 to 25 years, less after a few hail seasons. If yours is past 20 and needs more than one repair, replacement is usually the better spend.

Daylight or damp in the attic

Go up on a sunny afternoon. If you see light through the boards, or stains on the wood, water is getting in.

A sagging ridge or soft spots

A dip along the ridge or decking that feels soft underfoot means the wood underneath is wet. That needs new decking, not just new shingles. We'll tell you straight which one you need, with photos.

title: Metal or shingles? What a new roof really costs over 30 years
excerpt: Metal costs more to put on and less to own. Here's how the numbers work out for a typical Oklahoma City home.
content:
We fit both, so we've no reason to push one. Here's how they compare on a typical 2,000 square foot home.

Up front

Architectural shingles run about $11,000 to $15,000 fitted. A standing-seam metal roof is about $24,000 to $32,000. Metal is roughly twice the price on day one.

Over time

Shingles last 18 to 25 years here, so most homes need two shingle roofs in the time one metal roof lasts. Metal also holds up better to hail, and many insurers give a lower premium for a Class 4 impact-rated roof.

Comfort and noise

Metal reflects more heat, which helps your summer bills. Over solid decking with underlayment it's no louder in the rain than shingles.

Our honest advice

If you plan to stay ten years or more, metal usually wins. If you're selling soon, good shingles make more sense. Book a free inspection and we'll price both side by side.

title: How a roof insurance claim works, step by step
excerpt: From the first call to the final check: who does what, how long it takes, and what you'll pay.
content:
A storm claim can feel like a lot of paperwork. It's simpler than it looks, and we do most of it with you.

1. Inspection

We inspect the roof for free and send a photo report. If the damage is real, you file the claim with your insurer, usually online or by phone in ten minutes.

2. The adjuster's visit

Your insurer sends an adjuster. We meet them on the roof so nothing gets missed, and point out every hit in our report.

3. The estimate

The insurer sends an estimate of what they'll pay. If something is left out, like vents, flashing or gutters, we send them the photos and ask for it to be added.

4. The work

Once it's approved, most roofs are replaced in one or two days. You pay your deductible and nothing else for the work the claim covers.

5. The final check

Your insurer may hold back part of the payment until the work is done. We send them the completion photos and invoice so it's released quickly.
